images.caption: STONE MOUNTAIN PARK, Stone Mountain, Georgia, June 8, 2014 - The 66th Annual Conference of the National Guard Association of Georgia and Georgia Enlisted Association (EANGGA) Conference took place June 6-8 2014 at the Stone Mountain Marriott Evergreen Conference Center and Resort. Conference activities included golfing, professional and business development seminars. The conference's concluded with a formal dinner with dancing and award ceremony. images.filename: Maj. Gen. Butterworth speaks with Guardsmen (14384303516).jpg
images.caption: STONE MOUNTAIN PARK, Stone Mountain, Georgia, June 8, 2014 – Major Gen. Jim Butterworth, the Adjutant General of the Georgia National Guard spoke candidly with Georgia Soldiers of the Warrant Officer Corps during the 66th Annual Conference of the National Guard Association of Georgia and Georgia Enlisted Association (EANGGA) Conference June 6-8 2014 at the Stone Mountain Marriott Evergreen Conference Center and Resort. “You are OUR go-to experts, a specific entity of professionals we have tremendous confidence in,” Butterworth said of the men and women he calls “the finest of the best.” The three-day conference offered a fun agenda of golfing, dining and dancing but was punctuated with opportunities for professional and business development through seminars. The Airmen and Soldiers of Georgia were also able to hear from leadership from the National Guard Bureau and Georgia 7th District Congressman, Rob Woodall. (Georgia National Guard photo by Staff Sgt. Tracy J. Smith)

STONE MOUNTAIN PARK, Stone Mountain, Georgia, June 4, 2017 - The 69th Annual Conference of the Enlisted Association of the National Guard of Georgia (EANGGA) and the National Guard Association of Georgia took place June 2-4 2017 at the Stone Mountain Marriott Evergreen Conference Center and Resort. During the event, members received strategic leadership presentations from Gen. Joseph Lengyel Chief, National Guard Bureau, Lt. Gen Gary H. Cheek, Director, Army Staff and Maj. Gen. James K. Brown Jr., Deputy Commanding General (RC). Conference activities included golfing, professional and business development seminars. The conferences concluded with a formal dinner with dancing and award ceremony which included, officers being presented with the Terrell J. Reddick Leadership Award.

images.filename: Bulletin 426 Plate XXV A Stone Mountain GA.jpg
images.caption:
Plate XXV A, Original caption:  "Stone Mountain, a granite dome, DeKalb County, GA."
This was published in 1910, prior to the construction of the Confederate Memorial.
Text from the volume referring to this figure:

Stone Mountain, which is a huge doming ridge of granite (Pl. XXV, A), is situated about 16 miles east of Atlanta in DeKalb County. It is an elliptical boss, with its longer axis trending northeast and southwest and its steepest side facing northward. It rises 686 feet above the adjacent lowland plain of crystalline rocks, and measures 7 miles in circumference around its base. The present ridge is the unreduced remnant of a much larger granite mass. The evidence favoring this conclusion is the fact that a belt of the same granite reduced to the general level of the surrounding Tertiary Piedmont plain skirts the north, west, and south sides of the ridge with a width varying from a quarter of a mile to more than a mile.
The granite of Stone Mountain and the granite gneiss of the adjacent Lithonia area in the same county have had the widest distribution and are the best known of the Georgia granites outside of the State. From the time of their first opening, prior to the civil war, to within the last few years the quarrying of stone in these two areas formed practically the whole granite industry in Georgia. These are the largest granite quarries in Georgia and they yield a much larger output than any other areas in the State.
Numerous quarries yielding an excellent light-gray granite are worked along the western and southern flanks of the ridge. (See Pl. XXV, B.) The stone has been used most extensively for general building purposes, and almost as largely for street material in the form of blocks and curbing. Its very light color makes it undesirable for monument stock. It has been marketed in the principal towns and cities in the South and West.
images.alt:
Plate XXV A, Original caption:  "Stone Mountain, a granite dome, DeKalb County, GA."
This was published in 1910, prior to the construction of the Confederate Memorial.
Text from the volume referring to this figure:

Stone Mountain, which is a huge doming ridge of granite (Pl. XXV, A), is situated about 16 miles east of Atlanta in DeKalb County. It is an elliptical boss, with its longer axis trending northeast and southwest and its steepest side facing northward. It rises 686 feet above the adjacent lowland plain of crystalline rocks, and measures 7 miles in circumference around its base. The present ridge is the unreduced remnant of a much larger granite mass. The evidence favoring this conclusion is the fact that a belt of the same granite reduced to the general level of the surrounding Tertiary Piedmont plain skirts the north, west, and south sides of the ridge with a width varying from a quarter of a mile to more than a mile.
The granite of Stone Mountain and the granite gneiss of the adjacent Lithonia area in the same county have had the widest distribution and are the best known of the Georgia granites outside of the State. From the time of their first opening, prior to the civil war, to within the last few years the quarrying of stone in these two areas formed practically the whole granite industry in Georgia. These are the largest granite quarries in Georgia and they yield a much larger output than any other areas in the State.
Numerous quarries yielding an excellent light-gray granite are worked along the western and southern flanks of the ridge. (See Pl. XXV, B.) The stone has been used most extensively for general building purposes, and almost as largely for street material in the form of blocks and curbing. Its very light color makes it undesirable for monument stock. It has been marketed in the principal towns and cities in the South and West.
